**Yes, likely covered, subject to the policy's other criteria.** An adult with a BMI of 36 and type 2 diabetes meets the BMI and comorbidity requirements for sleeve gastrectomy. Under UnitedHealthcare's Bariatric Surgery policy, sleeve gastrectomy is proven and medically necessary for adults aged 18 or older when all the listed criteria are met. One option is a BMI of 35 to 39.9 kg/m² with at least one comorbidity, and insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes is one of those comorbidities [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

The full set of criteria for an adult is:

- **BMI:** either BMI ≥ 40 kg/m² (or ≥ 37.5 in individuals of Asian descent), or BMI 35 to 39.9 kg/m² (or 32.5 to 37.4 in individuals of Asian descent) with one or more listed comorbidities [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].
- **Comorbidity (for BMI 35 to 39.9):** insulin resistance or type 2 diabetes, or one of the other listed conditions, such as cardiovascular disease, poorly controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, OSA confirmed on polysomnography (AHI or RDI ≥ 30), or MASLD [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1] [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
- **Preoperative evaluation:** completion of a preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history, along with dietary and physical activity patterns [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
- **Psychosocial-behavioral evaluation:** a screening by a professionally recognized behavioral health discipline to identify risk factors or potential postoperative challenges, or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen. The policy lists these as alternatives [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].

The policy's coverage rationale also lists sleeve gastrectomy among the procedures it treats as proven for obesity, so the patient's documentation needs to show the BMI, the diabetes diagnosis and both evaluations. I haven't checked the policy's Benefit Considerations section, which the coverage rationale refers to, so benefit-level limits may apply.

For an adult of Asian descent with no other conditions, the policy's threshold is a **BMI of 37.5 kg/m² or higher**. For other adults the threshold is 40 kg/m² [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

The policy's sleeve gastrectomy criteria also require the following for adults:
- **Preoperative evaluation:** completion of a preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history, plus dietary and physical activity patterns [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
- **Psychosocial-behavioral evaluation** by a professional from a behavioral health discipline, or **participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].

The lower BMI option (35 to 39.9 kg/m², or 32.5 to 37.4 kg/m² for Asian descent) applies only with one of the listed comorbidities, so it does not apply to this patient [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

For an adult with no obesity-related comorbidities, the threshold is a **BMI of 40 kg/m² or greater**, or **37.5 kg/m² or greater for individuals of Asian descent** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. The policy places no comorbidity requirement on this BMI tier. Comorbidities are only needed for the lower BMI tier of 35 to 39.9 kg/m² (32.5 to 37.4 for Asian descent) [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

The policy also requires these conditions for adults, which apply to every patient:
- Age 18 years or older [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].
- The procedure is one of the covered bariatric procedures: biliopancreatic diversion with or without duodenal switch, gastric bypass, adjustable gastric banding, or sleeve gastrectomy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].
- Completion of a preoperative evaluation that includes a detailed weight history, along with dietary and physical activity patterns [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].
- Either a psychosocial-behavioral evaluation by a professional in a behavioral health discipline, to screen for risk factors or potential postoperative challenges, or participation in a multidisciplinary surgical preparatory regimen [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2].

Separately, the policy's Maryland-only benefit considerations list a BMI above 40 kg/m² without comorbidity as one qualifying option, and add a psychological examination and a structured diet program requirement [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.9].

No. The UnitedHealthcare Bariatric Surgery policy lists endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty as unproven and not medically necessary for treating obesity, due to insufficient evidence of efficacy. It appears under "Transoral endoscopic surgery, including: Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (includes OverStitch™)" [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

A planned two-stage bariatric procedure is proven and medically necessary when all of the following are met:

- **Initial BMI of ≥ 50 kg/m² before the first-stage procedure** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]
- **Second stage occurs within 2 years after the primary bariatric surgery** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]
- **The individual has been adherent to nutrition and exercise** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]
- **The individual meets the medical necessity criteria at the time of the second-stage procedure** [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

The two-stage criteria appear in the policy's section on adolescents aged 12 to 17, directly after the adolescent requirements for obesity class and a multidisciplinary evaluation [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]. The adult criteria in the policy don't mention two-stage procedures [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. The policy doesn't say whether the two-stage criteria also apply to adults. The "adherent to nutrition and exercise" wording replaced "compliant with nutrition and exercise" as of 05/01/2026 [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.55].

Yes. The policy states that removing an adjustable gastric band and all related components, when it does not result in a revisional surgery, is proven and medically necessary [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The removal code for the band component alone is 43772 [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.5].

No. The UnitedHealthcare Bariatric Surgery policy lists the intragastric balloon as unproven and not medically necessary for treating obesity, due to insufficient evidence of efficacy. It appears under "Transoral endoscopic surgery, including" in that list [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The policy also notes that FDA approval of a bariatric device alone is not a basis for coverage [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.43]. The FDA-approved Orbera balloon is indicated for adults with a BMI of 30 to 40 kg/m² who have failed conservative weight-reduction strategies [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.43].

No. The UnitedHealthcare Bariatric Surgery policy lists the mini-gastric bypass, also called laparoscopic mini-gastric bypass or one-anastomosis gastric bypass, among the bariatric interventions for obesity that are unproven and not medically necessary due to insufficient evidence of efficacy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The policy's covered procedures for obesity are biliopancreatic diversion with or without duodenal switch, gastric bypass, adjustable gastric banding, and sleeve gastrectomy, when the patient meets the policy's criteria [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

Adjustable gastric banding is covered as proven and medically necessary only for individuals 18 years of age or older [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]. The FDA section also states that adjustable gastric bands are contraindicated in patients younger than 18 years of age [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.44].

Revisional surgery for reflux after a sleeve gastrectomy is covered only when the reflux is uncontrollable and all three of these criteria are met:

1. **Maximum nonpharmacological medical management failure**, such as positional, dietary modification, or behavioral changes.
2. **Maximum pharmacological medical management failure**, such as at least 1 month of double-dose proton pump inhibitor, H2 blocker, and/or sucralfate.
3. **Severe esophagitis (grade C or D) confirmed by endoscopy** despite maximum medical management. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

Revisional bariatric surgery for any indication other than those listed in the policy is unproven and not medically necessary. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]

The CPT code for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy is **43775** (laparoscopy, surgical, gastric restrictive procedure; longitudinal gastrectomy, i.e., sleeve gastrectomy). The policy says to use 43775 rather than the unlisted laparoscopy code 43659 [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.4] [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.5].

CPT 43889 is the code for a transoral endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG), including argon plasma coagulation when performed [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.5].

UnitedHealthcare's Bariatric Surgery policy lists transoral endoscopic surgery, including endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (includes OverStitch), as unproven and not medically necessary for treating obesity, due to insufficient evidence of efficacy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3]. So this service is not covered under that policy.

For adults, sleep apnea counts as a qualifying comorbidity only when it is **obstructive sleep apnea confirmed on polysomnography with an Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) or Respiratory Disturbance Index (RDI) of 30 or more**. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.2]

This applies when the patient's BMI is 35 to 39.9 kg/m² (or 32.5 to 37.4 in individuals of Asian descent). A BMI of 40 or more qualifies without a comorbidity. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1]

The policy's severity definitions are: mild for AHI or RDI of 5 to under 15, moderate for 15 to 30, and severe for more than 30 per hour. [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.4] The coverage criterion uses "30 or more," so an AHI or RDI of exactly 30 meets the threshold even though the severity definitions place 30 in the moderate band.

No. UnitedHealthcare's bariatric surgery policy lists "bariatric surgery as the primary treatment for any condition other than obesity" as unproven and not medically necessary, due to insufficient evidence of efficacy [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].

The policy covers bariatric procedures only for treating obesity. The listed procedures (biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch, gastric bypass, adjustable gastric banding, and sleeve gastrectomy) are proven and medically necessary for treating obesity, and only when the obesity criteria are met [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

The policy defines Class II obesity in adolescents as **120% of the 95th percentile height or an absolute BMI of 35 to 39.9 kg/m², whichever is lower**. It attributes this classification to the American Society for Metabolic and Bariatric Surgery (Pratt et al., 2018) [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.3].
The UnitedHealthcare bariatric surgery policy is number 2026T0362RR, with an effective date of May 1, 2026 [uhc-bariatric-surgery.pdf p.1].

No. For a 7-month-old with single-sided sensorineural hearing loss, the policy treats non-hybrid cochlear implantation as experimental or investigational, so it is not covered.

The policy says non-hybrid cochlear implantation for single-sided or asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss is proven and medically necessary for children ages 9 months or older. For children younger than 9 months, it is experimental or investigational because the device lacks FDA approval for that use [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. The scanned copy of the policy says the same [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.1].

For children 9 months and older, the medical necessity criteria are in the InterQual CP: Procedures, Cochlear Implantation (Pediatric) criteria that the policy refers to [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. I did not find those criteria in the policy text, so I can't list them.

A non-hybrid cochlear implant is covered for a child with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss from **6 months of age**. [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]

Medical necessity for these children is judged against the InterQual CP: Procedures, Cochlear Implantation (Pediatric) criteria. [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]

Yes, for adults, but only under certain circumstances. The UnitedHealthcare Cochlear Implants policy states that hybrid cochlear implantation is "proven and medically necessary under certain circumstances for Sensorineural Hearing Loss in adults ages 18 and older" [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1] [uhc-cochlear-implants-scan.pdf p.1].

The policy refers to the InterQual® CP: Procedures, Cochlear Implantation criteria for medical necessity [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1]. The policy text I can search does not list the specific clinical conditions, so I can't tell you what those circumstances are. You would need to check the InterQual criteria themselves.

No. The cochlear implant policy says FM systems are excluded from coverage. They can be used as an extension or accessory of a cochlear implant, but they do not meet the definition of a covered health care service. The policy states they do not prevent, diagnose, or treat a sickness or injury, and are not integral to the function of the cochlear implant itself. [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]

The external speech processor is covered under the durable medical equipment (DME) benefit. The policy says cochlear implant external components, including the speech processor, microphone, and transmitter coil, are considered under the DME benefit, while the implantable components fall under the medical-surgical benefit [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].

For repair or replacement of external components, the member's specific benefit plan document determines whether DME benefits apply, and the Durable Medical Equipment, Orthotics, Medical Supplies, and Repairs/Replacements policy is referenced [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].
HCPCS L8619 is the **cochlear implant external speech processor and controller, integrated system, replacement** code. [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]
The CPT code for cochlear device implantation is **69930**, which is described as "Cochlear device implantation, with or without mastoidectomy" [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].

Under UnitedHealthcare's cochlear implant policy, remapping and reprogramming of the implant, and rehabilitation after the implant surgery, are covered as an outpatient rehabilitation therapy benefit. The policy notes this service is usually billed as aural rehabilitation [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2]. The member's specific benefit plan document must be checked for any limits that apply to aural rehabilitation [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.2].
The UnitedHealthcare Cochlear Implants policy is number **2026T0070II**, effective June 1, 2026 [uhc-cochlear-implants.pdf p.1].

Under UnitedHealthcare's Ambulance Services policy (MP.001.25), emergency air ambulance is considered medically necessary only when all three of the following criteria are present:

1. **Need for immediate transport that ground ambulance cannot provide.** The member's condition requires immediate transportation that cannot be provided by ground ambulance, and a delay may endanger the member's life or seriously endanger their health. This includes situations where:
   - ground transport times are excessive (about 30–60 minutes or longer); or
   - weather or traffic makes ground transport impractical, impossible, or overly time-consuming; or
   - the pickup point is inaccessible by ground ambulance and [the policy text is cut off here] [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]

2. **Destination.** The destination is the nearest acute care hospital that can meet the member's needs. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]

3. **Requesting authority or level of care.** One of the following exists:
   - services are requested by police or medical authorities at the site of an emergency; or
   - advanced or basic life support is required during transport. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]

Air ambulance is not medically necessary for any other indication. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1] Transport that does not meet these criteria is excluded. [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]

The policy doesn't set a fixed travel-time cutoff. It lists excessive ground transport time as one circumstance, described as "30-60 minutes or longer" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

Excessive ground time is one of several alternatives. Emergency air ambulance is medically necessary when all of these are present [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1]:

- **Medical need:** The member's condition requires immediate transportation that ground ambulance cannot provide, and a delay may endanger life or seriously endanger health. This applies when ground transport times are excessive (30-60 minutes or longer), when weather or traffic makes ground transport impractical, impossible, or overly time-consuming, or when the pickup point is inaccessible by ground ambulance.
- **Destination:** The destination is the nearest acute care hospital that can meet the member's needs.
- **Requesting or care level:** Either police or medical authorities request it at the scene of an emergency, or advanced or basic life support is required during transport.

The policy states that emergency air ambulance is not medically necessary for all other indications [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

No. Under UnitedHealthcare's Ambulance Services policy, a taxi or rideshare trip to the hospital is not covered, even when it's an emergency. The policy lists "Taxi ride, bus ride, rideshare services such as Lyft and Uber" as non-ambulance transportation that is "not covered even if rendered in an Emergency situation" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]. The same exclusion covers a police car ride to a hospital and medi-van or wheelchair van transportation [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Covered emergency transport is licensed ground ambulance, which is medically necessary when the member's condition requires immediate transportation to the nearest acute hospital that can treat the illness or injury [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

Yes. The UnitedHealthcare Ambulance Services policy states that prior authorization is required for non-emergency air ambulance transport [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]. The same policy notes that certain plans may also require prior authorization for non-emergency ground ambulance transport, and that coverage depends on the member's benefit plan document [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Non-emergency air ambulance transport is covered only between facilities and only when it meets one of the listed conditions, such as moving a patient from an out-of-network hospital to the closest network hospital when covered services are needed [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.5]. Air ambulance transport that does not meet the covered indications is not eligible for coverage [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Yes, in the case you describe, the ambulance service can be covered. The policy says emergency ground ambulance services without ground transportation are considered Medically Necessary when the emergency ground ambulance personnel render treatment at the scene [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2]. Emergency ground ambulance transportation is not considered Medically Necessary for other indications [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2].

The policy also lists HCPCS code A0998 (ambulance response and treatment, no transport) [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.5].

No. The Ambulance Services policy states that "ambulance transportation to a home, residential, domiciliary, or custodial facility is not covered" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6]. The policy also lists "hospital to home" as ambulance transportation deemed not appropriate [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

Out-of-network emergency ambulance transport (ground, water, or air) is covered at the network level of deductible and coinsurance, but only if the transport itself meets the policy's coverage criteria [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].

**Criteria for the transport to be covered:**

- **Emergency ground ambulance** is medically necessary when all of these are present:
  - The member's condition requires immediate transportation to the nearest acute hospital that can treat the illness or injury, to the nearest neonatal special care unit for qualifying newborn conditions, or to a hospital with a required higher level of care not available at the original hospital [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1] [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2].
  - A delay in transportation may endanger the member's life or seriously endanger their health [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2].
  - Advanced or basic life support is required during transport [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2].
  - Ground transport without a ride is covered when emergency personnel treat the member at the scene [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.2].
- **Emergency air ambulance** is medically necessary when all of these are present:
  - The condition requires immediate transport that ground ambulance cannot provide, and delay may endanger life or seriously endanger health. Examples include excessive ground transport times (30–60 minutes or longer), weather or traffic that makes ground transport impractical, or a pickup point ground ambulance cannot reach [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].
  - The destination is the nearest acute care hospital that can meet the member's needs [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].
  - Police or medical authorities requested it at the emergency scene, or advanced or basic life support is required during transport [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.1].

**Not covered regardless of network status:** Non-ambulance transport, even in an emergency (such as a police car, taxi, or rideshare), and ambulance transport when another mode would not endanger the member's health [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.6].
HCPCS A0998 means "Ambulance response and treatment, no transport." It is listed in the Ground/Other Ambulance code table of the Ambulance Services policy [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.5].

In UnitedHealthcare's Ambulance Services policy, the QL modifier means "patient pronounced dead after ambulance called" [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.4].

It is an exception to the usual billing format. Ambulance claims are normally billed with two modifiers, the first for the place of origin and the second for the destination. QL must be billed in place of that origin/destination pair [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.4].
HCPCS A0431 is "Ambulance service, conventional air services, transport, one way (rotary wing)." It is listed under Air Ambulance in the ambulance services policy [uhc-ambulance-services.pdf p.4].

No. UnitedHealthcare's Clinical Trials policy says its clinical trial benefits do not include the experimental or investigational service or item used in the trial [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3]. The exceptions are:

- **Certain FDA-designated Category B devices**, but only if all of these are met: the device is used within an FDA-approved clinical trial, it is used according to the trial's approved protocols, it falls under a covered benefit category and is not excluded by law, regulation or current Medicare coverage guidelines, it is medically necessary and used at a medically appropriate amount, duration and frequency, and it is furnished in a setting appropriate to the member's needs [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3].
- **Certain promising interventions for members with terminal illnesses** [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3].
- **Other items and services** that UnitedHealthcare determines meet its specified criteria under its medical and drug policies [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3].

What is covered are routine patient costs: services normally provided without a trial, when they are required solely for providing the investigational item (for example, the infusion administration to deliver an investigational drug), for clinically appropriate monitoring, or for preventing complications, along with reasonable and necessary care arising from the investigational service [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2].

No. UnitedHealthcare's Clinical Trials policy (MP.006.27) excludes travel and lodging costs for clinical trials. The policy lists "travel and transportation expenses," including fees for any type of transportation, rental cars, mileage reimbursement for a personal vehicle, lodging, and meals [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.3]. The billing codes for these services are also marked "Not Covered": S9992 for transportation, S9994 for lodging such as hotel charges, and S9996 for meals, each for the participant and one caregiver or companion [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.5].

An Approved Clinical Trial, for the cancer or life-threatening disease benefit, is a Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, or Phase IV clinical trial [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1]. Each phase must also be conducted in relation to the prevention, detection, or treatment of cancer or another life-threatening disease or condition, and must meet the Criteria for Approved Clinical Trials [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1].

A "life-threatening disease or condition" is one from which the likelihood of death is probable unless the course of the disease or condition is interrupted [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1].

The criteria require the trial to be described in one of the main bullets, such as being approved or funded by a listed body (for example NIH, CDC, AHRQ, or CMS), being conducted under an investigational new drug application reviewed by the FDA, or being an exempt drug trial [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2].

No, not solely because the trial is in another state. For an approved clinical trial conducted outside the member's state of residence, UnitedHealthcare "may not deny or otherwise limit payment for routine patient services solely on the basis that the trial is conducted out of state" [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2].

Other conditions in the policy still apply:

- **Qualifying trial and eligibility:** The PPACA routine-cost coverage applies to a Qualifying Individual in an Approved Clinical Trial, and benefits are available only when the covered person is clinically eligible for the trial as defined by the researcher [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.1].
- **Network participation:** If one or more network providers are participating in the trial, UnitedHealthcare may require the member to participate using a network provider, as long as that provider will accept the member as a participant [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2].
- **Non-life-threatening conditions:** For trials treating non-life-threatening diseases or conditions, routine-cost coverage is not mandated by PPACA. Coverage depends on whether the member's plan includes that benefit, so the member's plan document controls [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2].

The Q1 modifier identifies a **routine clinical service provided in a clinical research study that is in an approved clinical research study** [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.5]. Under the same table, a claim carrying this modifier is considered a Clinical Trials claim [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.5].

Not necessarily. For trials treating non-life-threatening diseases or conditions, UnitedHealthcare's policy says coverage of routine patient costs is not currently mandated by the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. Some UnitedHealthcare plans do include this coverage, so you need to check the member's specific benefit plan document for details [uhc-clinical-trials.pdf p.2].

Coma stimulation is not covered. The UnitedHealthcare Cognitive Rehabilitation and Coma Stimulation policy states that coma stimulation (also called coma arousal, coma responsiveness, multisensory stimulation, and coma care therapy/programs) is unproven and not medically necessary due to insufficient evidence of efficacy for any Disorder of Consciousness [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.1].

The policy's clinical evidence section also says that controlled trials of coma stimulation programs are limited and do not consistently show improved outcomes in people with disorders of consciousness [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.6]. That section is background, not the coverage rule.

Yes, outpatient cognitive rehabilitation is covered under certain circumstances. UnitedHealthcare's policy says it is "proven and medically necessary under certain circumstances" [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.1]. The policy does not list those circumstances in its Coverage Rationale. It refers to the InterQual® LOC: Outpatient Rehabilitation & Chiropractic criteria for medical necessity [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.1]. I did not have access to those InterQual criteria, so I can't state the specific conditions here.

The policy applies only to outpatient services. Inpatient services are addressed in the member's specific benefit plan document [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.1].

The CPT codes listed for cognitive rehabilitation in the UnitedHealthcare policy are:

- **97129**: Therapeutic interventions that focus on cognitive function (e.g., attention, memory, reasoning, executive function, problem solving, and/or pragmatic functioning) and compensatory strategies to manage the performance of an activity, direct (one-on-one) patient contact; initial 15 minutes [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.2]
- **97130**: The same service, direct (one-on-one) patient contact; each additional 15 minutes (listed separately in addition to the primary procedure code) [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.2]

The policy also lists HCPCS code S9056 (coma stimulation per diem), but that is for coma stimulation, which the policy describes as unproven and not medically necessary, not for cognitive rehabilitation [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.2] [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.1].

The code list is for reference only and may not be all-inclusive. Listing a code does not mean the service is covered [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.2].
HCPCS S9056 is coma stimulation, billed per diem. [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.2]

The cognitive rehabilitation policy does not address inpatient services. It applies to outpatient cognitive rehabilitation only, and it refers inpatient services to the member's specific benefit plan document [uhc-cognitive-rehabilitation.pdf p.1]. To find out whether a member's inpatient cognitive rehabilitation is covered, check that benefit plan document.

I searched for acupuncture, its billing codes, and back pain and alternative-medicine terms, and none of the results covered acupuncture. The policies I can search don't address this coverage question, so I can't say whether it is covered or not covered.

Your member's benefit plan document is the controlling source for coverage. Checking it, or calling UnitedHealthcare member services, would give a definitive answer.

Aetna's own medical policy or provider materials would have the answer. If you're looking for UnitedHealthcare's bariatric surgery requirements instead, I can search those.

I couldn't find CPT 99213 in the UnitedHealthcare policies I can search. A code lookup for 99213 returned no matches, and searches for office visits and established-patient evaluation and management found nothing that addresses it.

So I can't say whether it is covered. The policies I have don't address this code or routine office visits. Coverage is determined by the member's specific benefit plan document, so check that document or the plan's benefit summary for office visit coverage.
